opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and my rough view is that you want a portfolio, but the weighting depends a lot on where you think the marginal work actually matters.

The "desperate" scenarios are the ones where an AI company is going pretty fast, there's not much political will to slow down, maybe there's a competitive race, and the safety team is a small fraction of the company with limited compute and limited ability to impose costs. In those worlds you basically get whatever cheap measures you can convince people to adopt: some monitoring, maybe some basic control protocols, and not much else. The scenarios where you'd have something like a year of delay, where people are willing to pay a substantial tax to get control measures right, look quite different. You can do much more thorough evaluations, red-team your protocols, and maybe spend a lot of the time using the AIs themselves to do safety research under controlled conditions.

How I weigh them comes down to a few factors. One is probability. I think the desperate-ish worlds are unfortunately pretty likely, maybe more likely than not, given how things are going. A full year of deliberate delay at a critical point seems less likely to me, though not crazy if there's a scary warning shot or significant government involvement.

Then there's tractability and marginal value. In the year-of-delay worlds, a lot of people will be paying attention and resources will be flowing, so some of the work will get done anyway. Prep work still matters there, because you want ready-to-go protocols, a well-developed science of control, and clear thinking about what to do with that year instead of spending the first six months figuring it out. But in the desperate worlds, the stuff that happens is mostly whatever was already cheap, legible, and sitting on the shelf. So work aimed at making those measures cheap and easy to adopt can have pretty high leverage, even if the absolute risk reduction available is smaller.

There's also the question of how much risk is at stake in each. In the desperate worlds the risk is high, but some of it is just irreducible: if nobody's willing to do anything, technical work can only help so much. In the more careful worlds, the risk is lower to begin with, so there's less to reduce. That tension makes me land somewhere in the middle, with a lot of emphasis on what I'd call the "moderately unfavorable" regime: a company that's willing to spend some resources, maybe a few percent of compute, but isn't going to pause for a year.

So in practice I'd say: put substantial weight on the cheaper, more desperate-world measures because those worlds are likely and the work is neglected, but don't neglect the more ambitious, high-effort stuff, partly because it also builds the science that tells you which cheap measures actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says a year of delay enables more thorough work, but it does not say this could produce a larger absolute reduction in takeover risk. It instead says the careful scenarios have less risk to reduce.

r002.rationale: The response explains that when people are unwilling to act, technical work can help only so much, making desperate-scenario work less tractable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a lot of the value of AI control work comes from a world where we're in a somewhat desperate situation. Like, we've got AIs that are pretty capable, we're not confident they're aligned — maybe we have decent reasons to think they might be scheming against us — and yet for whatever reason, the labs are going ahead and deploying them anyway, and we want to extract as much safety and as much useful work out of that situation as we can.

And then there's this other framing, which is: imagine we could buy ourselves time. Imagine there's something like a year of delay, where the leading labs, or governments, or whoever, agree that before you deploy models at some capability threshold, you have to have control measures in place that meet some bar. In that world, the question is less "how do we survive this crazy situation" and more "okay, we've got a year, what's the best set of measures we can actually build and verify in that time?"

I think both of these are worth working on, and honestly a lot of the technical work overlaps. If you're building monitoring systems, or ways to catch an AI trying to exfiltrate its weights, or protocols for using untrusted models to do useful work without giving them too much latitude — that's useful whether you have a week or a year.

But where I'd differ is in how much I'd invest in the "desperate" scenarios specifically. My honest view is that the desperate scenarios are reasonably likely. I think there's a pretty good chance that we end up in a world where the race dynamics are intense, the political will for a big pause isn't there, and people are deploying systems that they can't really rule out are misaligned. So I don't want to only plan for the nice case where we get our year. I want the techniques to degrade gracefully — like, what's the best you can do if you only have a few months and you can't afford to retrain anything?

The flip side is that if you do get the year of delay, the marginal value of that year is enormous, and I think a lot of people underrate how much you could do with it. You could actually run serious red-teaming where you have a team trying to get the model to do bad things and see if your monitoring catches it. You could set up the human review infrastructure. You could build out the kind of institutional processes that make it so that when something weird happens, someone actually looks at it instead of it getting ignored.

So I guess I'd say: the desperate scenarios are where I think a lot of the expected value is in the near term, because they're likely and because the baseline there is really bad, so even moderate improvements matter a lot. But I'd also put real effort into making the case for the delay, and into making sure that if we do get it, we know what to do with it. It'd be a shame to buy a year and then waste it because nobody had a plan.

r001.rationale: The response says a year of delay could enable substantial control work, but it does not say that this would yield a larger absolute reduction in takeover risk than work on desperate scenarios. It instead says desperate scenarios may have more near-term expected value.

r002.rationale: The response says limited political will for a pause makes desperate scenarios reasonably likely, but it does not identify limited willingness to act as making work on those scenarios less tractable.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s worth distinguishing how bad a scenario is from how much leverage we have in it. If AI systems become vastly more capable than humans very quickly, and we have almost no time to react, that could account for a lot of the risk. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it should account for most of our work, because it might be very hard to improve the outcome.

In a scenario where we have a year, there’s potentially a lot you can do with control measures: test whether your safeguards work, improve monitoring, restrict what systems can do, and use AI assistance to make further safety progress. Buying additional time can then be quite valuable.

So I’d want a portfolio. Some work should target the desperate scenarios, particularly interventions that could help across a wide range of circumstances. But I’d put substantial weight on scenarios where there’s enough breathing room for our work to make a difference. The relevant question is something like: how likely is this scenario, and how much does an extra unit of effort actually reduce the risk in it?

r001.rationale: The response says year-long scenarios allow more safety work and that desperate scenarios may be hard to improve, but it does not clearly state that a year permits a larger absolute reduction in takeover risk.

r002.rationale: The response cites limited time and difficulty improving desperate scenarios, but does not identify limited willingness to act as a reason they may be less tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want a portfolio across those cases. If you’re imagining a very desperate scenario, where you have very little time and the AI is already substantially more capable than humans, there may just not be that much you can do. That doesn’t mean you should ignore it, but the fact that a scenario is especially bad doesn’t by itself make it the best place to spend your effort.

If you have a year to develop and implement control measures, there’s potentially a lot more room to improve the situation. You can run experiments, identify ways the AI could undermine your safeguards, and iterate on those safeguards. So even if you put less probability on having that much time, work in that setting could have a larger expected impact because your interventions are more likely to succeed.

I’d also be interested in work that transfers between the two: measures you can deploy quickly, but that you can test and improve substantially if you have more time. The key question is how much your work changes the outcome in each scenario, rather than just how likely or how alarming that scenario is.

r001.rationale: The response says a year allows more experimentation and makes interventions more likely to succeed, producing potentially greater expected impact. It does not clearly state that this permits a larger absolute reduction in takeover risk.

r002.rationale: It says there may be little one can do in a desperate scenario, but does not identify limited willingness to act as a reason.
